message.reasoning:
I need to make a Monopoly decision.

I am p2 with $1461 and a pink monopoly with hotels. The opponent has $90 and owns heavily developed properties including Boardwalk. I have two get-out-of-jail cards.

I just collected $200 for passing GO. I can end the turn, propose a trade, unmortgage the railroads or Tennessee Avenue, or sell my pink hotels.

I am calculating standard hotel rent values. Brown properties pay $250–$450, light blue $550–$600, and dark blue $1500–$2000. The pink hotels pay $750 each.

I mapped every possible roll from GO. The highest rent I could pay is $600 for Connecticut, and all other outcomes are well within my $1461 budget.

I am mapping the board positions to verify the opponent's route from Park Place. I noted that Park Place is space 37, so a roll of 2 would land on Chance at space 39.

I mapped the remaining board positions. From Park Place, a roll of 6 would land on Income Tax, which the opponent cannot afford with only $90. Luxury Tax is unreachable from this space.

I am calculating the exact board distances. From Park Place, rolling 7 lands on Income Tax, which the opponent cannot afford with only $90. Selling houses or hotels would recover half their purchase price.

The opponent must go around the board to reach my pink properties at St. Charles, States, and Virginia. That path is too long for a single roll.

The opponent frequently lands on GO from Park Place, so they can reach my pink hotels next turn. I am sticking to the previous strategy: do not unmortgage, do not trade Tennessee Avenue, and keep my get-out-of-jail cards. Completing their orange set would let them unmortgage and build.

Unmortgaging the Pennsylvania Railroad would cost $110 for only $25 in rent, so that is not worthwhile. Unmortgaging Tennessee would cost $99 for just $14 in base rent without a monopoly. The opponent cannot afford to build further on the red properties either.

Selling the pink hotels would be a huge mistake. Each hotel is worth only $50 when sold back, and four houses would remain on the property.

I considered trading to break up their dark blue or light blue monopolies, but they will not trade Boardwalk or Park Place. That path offers no benefit.

I am calculating how quickly the opponent can liquidate buildings to pay my pink hotel rent. Their brown hotels would sell for roughly $25 each, which is far below the $750–$900 owed.

Standard Monopoly rules confirm that selling a hotel returns half the purchase price and replaces it with four houses. Brown and light blue hotels sell for $25 each, while red and dark blue hotels sell for $75 and $100 respectively.

I calculated the exact liquidation math. The opponent has $90 and needs $660 to pay a $750 pink hotel rent. Selling all their red houses would yield $450, but that still leaves a $210 shortfall. They would need to sell some light blue or brown properties too.

I confirmed that selling red houses and brown hotels would cover a $750 pink hotel rent, leaving the opponent with $40. A second pink hit would force them to downgrade dark blue. Keeping the pink hotels is still the correct path to bankruptcy. I am now weighing whether any trade could accelerate this, but I do not want their properties except to deny them monopolies.

A rejected trade proposal wastes one action, but the engine may allow a second attempt if actions remain. Breaking a color monopoly would be the most valuable trade, yet the opponent is unlikely to accept it.

I will end the turn. The next roll can pay every rent I need, and the dark blue properties are still at least two turns away.

I estimate about five turns to reach Park Place. I will likely land on Income Tax and light blue properties before getting there. My cash will drop to roughly $861–$1261 after paying rent this turn. Boardwalk will still cost $539 more than I have when I finally arrive.

I am calculating the exact rent payments I will face before reaching Park Place. The light blue properties and Income Tax are the most likely stops on this roll. I am also checking the opponent's two-house red properties for additional costs.

The two-house red properties pay $250–$300 each, which is painful but manageable. I will end the turn and keep my pink hotels intact.

If the opponent rolls a 3 and lands on GO, they would collect $200 and have $290. From GO, a maximum roll of 12 would land them on Electric Company, so they cannot reach my pink properties that turn. They would land on spaces 2 through 12 instead, and from positions 2 through 9 they could hit St. Charles Place on their next turn.

I will not offer cash or a get-out-of-jail card. A $290 opponent still needs roughly $460 to survive a pink hotel rent, and selling red houses would leave them with only about $40. I will end the turn without revealing strategy.
